transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Blue Harbor - Head of ML), Sofia Ramirez (Blue Harbor - Platform Eng), Daniel Lee (Blue Harbor - CTO)

Summary: Kickoff to align on latency SLO definitions and a measurement plan. Customer wants clear acceptance boundaries for first-token latency vs per-token throughput, plus a sampling plan that captures tail behaviour for their multimodal assistant. Redwood will provide harness and initial scripts; customer to provide traces.

--- Optional auto-sections ---
Topics covered (quick): TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99, burstiness, warm vs cold KV cache, batch sizing, quantized model tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, security gating (SOC2, SSO, KMS), timeline ~6 weeks for pilot.
Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey all, thanks for making time, we wanted to run through acceptance criteria and the measurement plan for the POC. I'm Maya from Redwood, liam's on the call to cover the deep performance bits.
[00:18] Evan: Thanks Maya, yeah our team has been looking at first-token latency impact on user engagement so TTFT's really top-of-mind, but we also need to ensure throughput at scale for batch exports.
[00:30] Liam: Totally, and often the right answer is a hybrid — you can set a TTFT SLO for interactive routes and TPOT for bulk or background jobs. We should map routes to SLO types.
[00:42] Sofia: Quick context — our traffic today: roughly 12 req/s steady, 250 req/s bursts; payloads vary 300B to 60KB. Also a ~20% tail of large multimodal requests. That's why we want p99 to be realistic.
[01:00] Daniel: From infra side, security is a gating factor — we need VPC + KMS, SOC2 attestation, and audit logs before anything goes production. For the POC we can accept redacted traces but we need to see the audit log flow.
[01:18] Liam: Understood. For measurement, we'll need sample slices that represent steady-state, burst, and cold-cache scenarios. We recommend including prefix-cached runs to show best-case and cold-start runs to see worst-case.
[01:33] Evan: When you say prefix cache you mean our existing KV cache usage, right?
[01:36] Liam: Yeah, the KV cache — sorry sometimes our transcripts say "kay-vee cash" — we mean the key-value attention cache. Prefixes where user conversations already have a cached context will reduce token generation time.
[01:46] Maya: To make this concrete, what SLO numbers should we be discussing? Evan, you mentioned TTFT sensitivity — is your product target p95 TTFT under 300ms? p99 under 600?
[02:00] Evan: We were thinking p95 ~250ms and p99 < 800ms for interactive. That said, we do not expect that for the heavy multimodal route; maybe we target p95 700ms and p99 1500ms there.
[02:12] Liam: Okay those are reasonable starting points. For TPOT, we usually measure per-token cost and average throughput; for batch workloads we'd target sustained 2k tokens/s with 95% of windows above 1.5k tokens/s — but that's model and hardware dependent.
[02:28] Sofia: Can you explain how you compute TPOT in the harness? We have seen different definitions across vendors.
[02:34] Liam: Good question. Our TPOT is tokens-per-second observed at the model boundary excluding network overhead; we also emit end-to-end metrics so you can compare. In the harness we run synthetic sequences drawn from your payload distribution, including the same stop conditions and streaming behavior you use.
[02:51] Daniel: We want both host-level numbers and end-to-end (client) numbers because network and gateway layers matter for our SLA.
[02:58] Maya: We'll produce both. The plan: Redwood will run two phases — microbenchmarks (isolated model runtime) and end-to-end runs (service + network + routing). We'll provide the harness to run locally or in your environment.
[03:13] Evan: How do you handle quantized model performance? Our initial tests used a 4-bit quantized variant and we saw weird tail spikes.
[03:21] Liam: Quantization can change kernel behavior and tail latency due to memory bandwidth / kernel scheduling. In our harness we include configurations for FP16 and int4 quantized paths and recommend including both in acceptance criteria.
[03:33] Sofia: For cold cache tests, what's a realistic cache drop frequency? We have many parallel users and KV cache warmup times differ.
[03:42] Liam: We recommend a cold-cache sweep that simulates an 8-hour window of idlethen burst to replicate long-tail users. Also a continuous churn scenario where 5-10% of requests miss the prefix cache.
[03:54] Evan: Regarding sampling, we can supply 7 days of traces — what format do you need?
[03:58] Maya: CSV of timestamp, route, payload_size_bytes, user_id_hash, model_requested, observed_latencies if available. If you can provide 72-hour full request traces as ndjson that'd be ideal. We'll accept redacted bodies.
[04:15] Daniel: Security note — we may need a DPA addendum to send traces with PII even if redacted. Sofia will follow up with legal.
[04:21] Sofia: Yep, we'll coordinate.
[04:24] Liam: Back to SLOs — for acceptance, we propose two tiers: 1) interactive routes: TTFT p95 <= 300ms (target), p99 <= 800ms (target), 2) multimodal/heavy routes: TTFT p95 <= 800ms, p99 <= 1600ms. And TPOT for batch: average tokens/s >= targetX with 95th percentile windows above threshold. We need you to approve these ranges or adjust.
[04:52] Evan: Those look fine as a starting hypothesis. We need to also include degradation policy: if p99 breaches, what's our fallback? We prefer graceful degradation via model variant fallback rather than circuit breaker.
[05:03] Maya: Redwood supports automatic fallback to a smaller quantized model or regional fallback. We'll include a canary roll and fallback policy in the POC runbook.
[05:12] Sofia: One more thing — we do have an internal cost target. If your suggested config reduces latency but multiplies cost by 4x, we need to know that tradeoff.
[05:21] Liam: We'll produce a cost/per-token estimate per configuration and include a tradeoff matrix. For each benchmark run, you'll get latency curves and unit-cost estimate.
[05:30] Evan: On instrumentation, can you emit both p95/p99 and distributions? We want heatmaps per-route.
[05:36] Maya: Yes, we will provide distribution histograms, bucketed tails, and time-series so you can see intermittency vs sustained issues.
[05:43] Daniel: Timeline? How long until we have the first set of benchmark results?
[05:48] Maya: If we get traces by Friday, Redwood can push an initial microbenchmark within 48 hours and an end-to-end run within 5 business days. That maps to the 6 week pilot if we add policy tuning and a second run.
[05:59] Evan: Sounds good. For acceptance criteria we want explicit sampling: 1M requests sampled across steady and burst windows with a dedicated subset for large payloads.
[06:09] Liam: We'll define sample sizes per route. For p99 confidence we usually target N>=10k samples per route slice, and higher for the multimodal tail. We'll include power calculations in the plan.
[06:20] Sofia: Can the harness run in our VPC? We need to see KMS integration and audit log flow.
[06:25] Maya: Yes, the harness can be run in your VPC via a deployment manifest. For KMS we support customer-managed keys and can integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll include instructions and a checklist.
[06:36] Evan: Are there any gotchas with batch sizes vs latency? We've seen larger batch windows decrease per-token cost but increase tail latency.
[06:44] Liam: Exactly. It's a tradeoff — for interactive SLOs we keep max batch sizes low and prefer continuous batching with latency-aware cutoffs. For batch jobs you can accept larger batches for throughput. The harness will sweep batch size to produce a latency vs cost frontier.
[06:58] Daniel: We need the result artifacts to be reproducible — scripts, seed configs, and the exact model commit.
[07:04] Liam: We'll include container images, model hash, and the kernel/compilation flags used. Reproducibility is a first-class deliverable.
[07:11] Evan: On reporting, can you provide an acceptance dashboard with p95/p99 per-route and a pass/fail flag?
[07:17] Maya: Yes. We'll produce a short dashboard and a deliverable report with pass/fail rows and suggested mitigations for failing routes.
[07:24] Sofia: What about noisy neighbors in Dedicated environments? If we go dedicated, will we be isolated?
[07:30] Maya: Dedicated capacity gives you GPU pool isolation; we also run interference tests in the harness to surface noisy neighbor effects. For Private on-prem we'll work with infra for placement and limits.
[07:41] Evan: Any limitations on streaming responses and function-calling latency?
[07:46] Liam: Streaming adds complexity; TTFT for streaming is measured to first stream chunk emission. Function-calling adds parsing overhead; we'll include the exact client-side patterns in the harness so the numbers match production.
[07:58] Daniel: Okay, let's recap responsibilities.
[08:00] Maya: Recap - Redwood: share harness and microbenchmark scripts, run initial microbench, run E2E if traces provided, produce dashboard and cost matrix. Customer: provide traces and security contact, approve SLO hypothesis or propose adjustments.
[08:15] Evan: Agree. One more question — do you have a recommended rolling window for p99 calculation? We use 1-minute windows today and it's noisy.
[08:22] Liam: We report both instantaneous p99 (1-minute) and aggregated p99 over 1-hour windows to reduce noise. We'll include both so you can choose.
[08:31] Sofia: OK thanks. We'll get the traces ready and legal will review the DPA.
[08:35] Maya: Great. We'll send the harness link and an initial measurement plan by Wednesday. Any other blockers?
[08:40] Evan: Not from us.
[08:42] Daniel: None here.
[08:43] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the next 48 hours with artifacts and proposed dates for the first benchmark run.

[58:00] End of recording
